title: China says US broke leaders' 'consensus' with first Cuba-linked sanctions on Chinese firms
dek: Beijing reserves the right to retaliate after Washington blacklisted two Chinese electronics suppliers for arming Cuba's military, three days before a rare-earth truce deadline. For India, the case is a reminder of how far US third-country sanctions now reach.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China's Ministry of Commerce said on Saturday that it "firmly opposes" new US sanctions on two Chinese companies accused of supplying Cuba's armed forces, and that Beijing "reserves the right to take necessary measures" in response. It said Washington had "deviated from the important consensus reached by the two heads of state", a reference to the trade truce between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump.

The dispute comes at a delicate moment. China's suspension of its sweeping October 2025 rare-earth export controls is due to lapse on 10 November with no published extension, and Mr Xi and Mr Trump are expected to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. It is the first time, according to reports, that the United States has sanctioned Chinese companies on Cuba-related grounds.

## What happened

The US State Department announced the measures on Thursday, 5 November, US time, in a fact sheet titled "Further Sanctions on the Cuban Regime's Foreign Military Support and Illicit Revenue Networks". According to reports of the announcement, it designated eight entities, two individuals and five vessels under Executive Order 14404, which Mr Trump signed on 1 May 2026 to target people linked to repression in Cuba and to threats to US national security.

The two Chinese companies are China National Electronics Import and Export Corporation (CEIEC), a state-owned exporter of defence electronics and security systems, and Beijing H&C Technologies, which reports describe as a subsidiary of the international arm of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (CETC), China's main state military-electronics group. The State Department said, according to reports, that both supplied military components and equipment to Cuba's Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces through Sociedad Mercantil Duna, a Cuban trading company that Washington sanctioned in August for arranging arms imports from China and Russia.

The same action covered shipping companies registered in Cyprus, Panama and Cuba that are linked to Cuba's oil trade, two Cuban state electronics and technical-services firms, and a relative of the head of GAESA, the military-run conglomerate that controls much of Cuba's economy. Reports said the Treasury also issued a determination that foreign firms working in Cuba's manufacturing, technology, electronics and maritime sectors may now be sanctioned. The State Department said the measures targeted "the regime and those who facilitate it, not the Cuban people", and that trade in food, medicine and medical devices remains authorised.

The Declaration could not open the State Department's fact sheet directly; the details above are as reported.

## Beijing's response

A commerce ministry spokesperson, answering a media question, said: "The US has imposed unilateral sanctions on Chinese companies on the grounds of their involvement with a third party, in violation of international law and basic norms of international relations. China firmly opposes such a move." The spokesperson said the United States had recently "intensified sanctions and pressure on China" with a series of "discriminatory and restrictive measures", and urged Washington "to correct its wrongful practices as soon as possible".

The ministry did not say what it might do. China has a set of tools it has used against US companies before: an Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law passed in 2021, an "unreliable entity list" that can bar foreign firms from trading with or investing in China, and export controls. Beijing has not responded to the substance of the US charge that the two firms supplied Cuba's military.

## Background

CEIEC is not new to US sanctions. The US Treasury designated it in November 2020 for helping the government of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela with digital surveillance and censorship technology. CETC, the parent group of Beijing H&C's owner, has been on US trade blacklists for years.

Washington has steadily tightened its Cuba policy since Mr Trump returned to office in 2025, aiming at the military-run companies that earn hard currency for the government in Havana. In July a State Department report said China operates three of Cuba's 18 signals-intelligence facilities, according to reports, and called this an "acute risk" to US military security. China and Cuba are close partners, and Beijing has long opposed the US embargo on the island.

The new measures land just as both sides are watching each other's deadlines under the truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025. On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in a video call that China must carry out its commitments "fully and immediately". The US suspension of its own "affiliates rule", which extends export restrictions to companies majority-owned by blacklisted firms, ends on 9 November, a day before China's rare-earth pause runs out.

## Why it matters for India

The case shows how US sanctions increasingly reach companies in third countries over their dealings with a sanctioned state, the very practice Beijing objected to on Saturday. Indian companies have been on the receiving end. Since 2024 the United States has designated several Indian-registered firms over trade in Iranian oil and petrochemicals and over supplies to Russia's military industry, and in August 2025 it imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods, citing India's purchases of Russian oil. Indian refiners cut back on Russian crude after the US sanctioned Russia's two largest oil producers, Rosneft and Lukoil, in October 2025.

A new US-China sanctions fight would also matter for India's supply chains. India relies on China for rare-earth magnets, electronics components, solar equipment and pharmaceutical ingredients. If Beijing answers with export controls rather than targeted listings, Indian manufacturers could be caught in the middle, as they were in 2025 when Chinese licences for rare-earth magnets were held up for months.

India has consistently voted at the UN General Assembly for resolutions calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, and New Delhi says it follows only sanctions imposed by the UN Security Council.

## What happens next

- 9 November: the US suspension of its affiliates rule is due to end.
- 10 November: China's suspension of its October 2025 rare-earth export controls is due to lapse unless Beijing publishes an extension.
- 18-19 November: APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen, where Mr Xi and Mr Trump are expected to hold talks; China has said it is discussing a three-way meeting that would include Russia's President Vladimir Putin.

Whether Beijing names any US company in retaliation before those dates will show how much weight it gives to Saturday's warning.
